title: Ice-dynamic regime of the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream derived from the mass flux balance of englacial units
abstract: An assumption commonly used for ice streams in ice sheet models is that the vertical profile of horizontal velocity is constant throughout the ice column from the surface to the base.Here, we use airborne radar data for mass flux balance analysis of the central part of the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream, to ascertain whether this assumption is broadly applicable in the ice stream's central region where the ice flow appears to be channelled by a large subglacial trough.We investigate the along-flow evolution of mass flux balance of both the full ice thickness and three englacial units in steady-state, and analyse the spatial variation of their imbalances.We assess the potential over-and under-estimation of ice flow velocity within the ice column and infer vertical shear profile models for our study region.These inferences suggest that the ice stream in this central region is flowing as a block, or plugflow, rather than with deformation from internal shearing, despite large variations in bed topography, basal shear stresses, and in a region with relatively slow ice flow velocities.

title: Permafrost carbon–climate feedback amplifies Earth system tipping risks
abstract: Abstract Global warming leads to widespread permafrost thaw and subsequent emissions of carbon dioxide and methane, driving the permafrost carbon–climate feedback (PCF) which amplifies climate change. Many current-generation climate models omit this feedback, limiting projections of long-term temperature outcomes and associated Earth system tipping risks. Here, we investigate how this feedback affects the risk and timing of crossing tipping points in the Earth system by integrating permafrost carbon emissions into temperature projections for idealized stabilization and overshoot scenarios. In a conceptual network model of interacting climate tipping elements—including the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, and the Amazon rainforest, we find that PCF leads to additional warming that increases the probability of exceeding one or more tipping elements by up to 50% and can substantially accelerate the timing of tipping events by hundreds of years. The effect of PCF on tipping risk and acceleration is particularly evident in overshoot scenarios with lower peak temperatures below 2–3 ∘ C or peak cumulative emissions of below 2000 PgC. Considering PCF, therefore, narrows the critical temperature space for overshoot pathways. Our results highlight that failing to account for PCF underestimates both climate risks and the urgency of mitigation, increasing the likelihood of tipping events across the Earth system.

title: Centennial-scale intensifications of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation during Heinrich Stadial 1
abstract: Centennial-scale changes in Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) strength might disturb global climate by altering interhemispheric heat transport and CO2 partitioning between the ocean and the atmosphere. Due to the short instrumental record and lack of high-resolution paleo records that so far only resolve millennial-scale changes, centennial-scale changes remain elusive. Here we use radiocarbon ventilation ages from a western equatorial Atlantic sediment core with a remarkably high sedimentation rate to reconstruct AMOC variability during the last deglaciation, with a focus on Heinrich Stadial 1 (HS1; 17.8-14.8 ka). Results from model simulations indicate that ventilation ages serve as a sensitive proxy for AMOC variability under weak overturning conditions (i.e., during HS1) at our study location. Notably, within an overall weakened AMOC condition during HS1, our record shows two centennial-scale AMOC intensifications: one from 16.5 to 15.8 ka and another at ~15.4 ka. These centennial-scale episodes of intensified AMOC briefly revitalized Atlantic interhemispheric heat transport during HS1, resulting in decreased precipitation over northeastern Brazil and short-lived but intense changes in climate elsewhere. These episodes of AMOC intensification likely transported substantial volumes of CO2-rich water from the mid-depth Atlantic to the Southern Ocean, where the CO2 was rapidly outgassed to the atmosphere. Using radiocarbon ages from Atlantic sediments, AMOC variability during Heinrich Stadial 1 is reconstructed, revealing brief intensifications that altered heat transport, reduced rainfall over northeastern Brazil, and likely enhanced atmospheric CO2.

title: Repeated loss of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet’s Amundsen Sea sector during late Pleistocene interglacials
abstract: Abstract Sea-level reconstructions and numerical models suggest that the vulnerable West Antarctic Ice Sheet underwent major mass losses during the late Pleistocene, raising global sea level by several metres. However, direct evidence from ice-sheet proximal records for such retreat has remained inconclusive. Here we investigate variations in clay mineral assemblages and past ocean temperatures archived in West Antarctic continental margin sediments during the last 800,000 years. Our results demonstrate that the supply of glacigenic detritus sourced from the main outlet glaciers in the Amundsen Sea sector of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet ceased almost entirely during all previous warm periods, documenting the loss of their drainage basins. Concomitant seawater warming, revealed by a microfossil proxy, is attributed to intensified deep-water advection towards Antarctica’s Pacific margin, which is corroborated by the clay mineralogical evidence. Our findings show that ocean forcing can drive major deglaciation of West Antarctica and related global sea-level rise.

title: Millennial-scale variability in Greenland dust provenance during Dansgaard–Oeschger events of the last glacial period
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Greenland ice-core records show an approximately 15-fold increase in dust concentration during cold stadial periods compared to warmer interstadial periods in the last glacial period (LGP). While multiple regions including East Asian deserts and the Sahara have been suggested as potential source areas (PSAs) for Greenland dust, millennial-scale variability of their relative contributions associated with Dansgaard–Oeschger climatic fluctuations during the LGP remains poorly constrained. To address this, we investigate high-resolution (~800 y) Pb and Sr isotopic, mineralogical, and geochemical records from the North Greenland Eemian Ice Drilling ice-core samples covering the entire LGP. We found that the Pb and Sr isotopic compositions, kaolinite-to-chlorite ratios, and chemical index of alteration values were higher during stadials than during interstadials. Comparison with PSAs suggests that East Asian deserts remained the dominant contributors to Greenland dust throughout the LGP, but contributions from the Sahara increased during stadial intervals. This shift likely reflects climate-driven changes in atmospheric circulation patterns responsible for transporting dust to Greenland. Our findings provide insights into the relationship between dust cycle dynamics and abrupt climate changes on millennial timescales during the LGP.

title: Polar ocean–cryosphere dynamics across past, present, and future climate states: AWI research highlights 2021–2025
abstract: The polar regions play a central role in the Earth system through their influence on ocean circulation, ice sheets, sea level, carbon cycling, and climate variability. Rapid anthropogenic warming is transforming these regions, highlighting the need to understand the processes, feedbacks, and thresholds that govern ocean–cryosphere interactions across a wide range of timescales. Here we synthesize major scientific advances achieved at the Alfred Wegener Institute during 2021–2025 within the Helmholtz research program Changing Earth – Sustaining Our Future. Combining paleoclimate archives, sustained observations, process studies, and Earth-system modeling, these studies provide new insights into the sensitivity of the climate system under past, present, and future climate conditions. Key findings include new constraints on Antarctic Ice Sheet evolution during past greenhouse climates, improved understanding of links between Southern Ocean circulation and climate–carbon feedbacks, advances in reconstructing Northern Hemisphere ice-sheet dynamics and deglaciation processes, and evidence that regional climate variability is stronger and more persistent than represented in many current climate models. Observations and simulations further reveal accelerating changes in Greenland outlet glaciers, important couplings between cryospheric change and the carbon cycle, and a growing role of mesoscale ocean dynamics in shaping future Arctic and global climate change. Together, these results demonstrate the value of integrating observations, paleoclimate evidence, and high-resolution modeling to constrain Earth-system sensitivity, identify critical feedbacks, and improve projections of future climate change in a warming world.

title: Solid-Earth geophysics and geodesy in Antarctica: achievements, current capabilities, and future directions
abstract: The Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) plays a major role in the global climate, providing a natural laboratory to study the processes that interlink the cryosphere, solid Earth, atmosphere, and hydrosphere. Through its ongoing mass loss, the AIS currently contributes to global-mean sea-level rise at a rate of 0.4 mm a −1 . However, its impact on and feedback with climate and sea-level changes are still poorly understood. To generate reliable sea-level projections for the future, there is an urgent need to substantially improve our knowledge of the solid-Earth properties and subsequent response to ice-mass variations in space and time. This issue has been identified as a key question by the international community, strongly supported by the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research (SCAR). We review how state-of-the-art Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) and seismic networks in Antarctica, in combination with further ground-based, airborne and satellite-based geophysical measurements, have been used to significantly advance our understanding of solid-Earth processes and their impact on the cryosphere. Future research activities should be coordinated to answer the most urgent science questions. For example, how can we consistently test and model, respectively, a realistic mantle rheology that includes lateral inhomogeneity and transient relaxation, together with AIS mass changes on all time scales since the Last Glacial Maximum, including Holocene retreat and readvance? What processes and boundary conditions should coupled ice-sheet/gravity-rotation-deformation models include in order to realistically reflect the complex interaction between the solid Earth, ice sheet and ocean? Based on the recent achievements and the most urgent science questions, a vision is articulated for science-driven, multidisciplinary geophysical observations and corresponding technological developments. Long-term observations and improved modelling must be combined to develop precise and reliable projections for Antarctica's future mass change and associated contribution to sea-level change at both regional and global scales.

title: Dominant Factor in the Relationship Between Ice Thickness and Flow Velocity in the Downstream Region of Shirase Glacier, East Antarctica, Derived from Remotely Sensed Data
abstract: The buttressing effect of landfast sea ice is crucial for the stability of Antarctic outlet glaciers. This study investigated spatiotemporal variations in flow velocity and ice thickness at the Shirase Glacier, East Antarctica, from 2016 to 2025 using ALOS-2/PALSAR-2 and CryoSat-2/SIRAL data. Flow velocity increased, and ice thickness decreased downstream, exhibiting a significant negative correlation (r = −0.66, p < 0.05). Notably, during periods of unstable landfast ice (2017–2018 and 2023–2025), substantial ice flow acceleration occurred in the downstream ice tongue. Furthermore, basal melt rates calculated using the Eulerian flux divergence method revealed high melting (16–20 m a−1) near the grounding line, decreasing to 2–4 m a−1 mid-stream, and increasing to 4–8 m a−1 near the ice front. This distribution is consistent with the subglacial oceanic vertical thermal structure. These results quantitatively demonstrate the significant control of both landfast ice stability and subglacial ocean circulation on the spatiotemporal dynamics of the Shirase Glacier.

title: Ice surface change drives subglacial hydrologic reorganization and interior speedup in northwest Greenland
abstract: Abstract Changes in ice surface elevation and slope influence subglacial water pressure and sliding velocity. Leveraging changes in elevation observed by the Ice, Cloud and land-Elevation satellite (ICESat) and ICESat-2 missions, we use coupled subglacial hydrology–ice dynamics modeling applied to a section of the northwest Greenland ice sheet to explore (i) how decadal-scale changes in ice surface elevation influence changes in winter background subglacial hydrology and corresponding ice velocity, and (ii) how much seasonal response is attributable to geometry versus environmental forcing. Our simulations suggest complex reorganization of the subglacial hydrologic system between 2004 and 2020, resulting from changes in surface elevation, driving redistribution of freshwater flux, an overall acceleration trend in the interior and an increase in background basal melt. Without changing hydrological conditions, geometry changes alone lead to greater interior acceleration, suggesting that changes in the subglacial system help to mitigate this speedup. We also find that the winter background state of the subglacial system modulates the seasonal response. This work demonstrates feedbacks that influence mass loss from the Greenland ice sheet as surface elevation evolves, highlighting the subtleties involved in accounting for changes in effective pressure, ice velocity and basal melt due to changes in subglacial hydrology.

title: Stochastic coupling of climate variables and ice volume over the Late Pleistocene glacial cycles
journal: Chaos An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science
abstract: Understanding the interactions between ice sheets and global climate forcings over geological timescales is essential for projecting their future. Previous studies have highlighted the role of ice dynamics and climate interactions in establishing the 100 000-year glacial cycles, particularly regarding the growth of North American ice sheets. Researchers have reconstructed consistent time series for ice volume, temperature, and carbon dioxide by applying inverse forward modeling to benthic oxygen isotope records. In this paper, we model the stochastic behavior of paleoclimate time series to evaluate the coupling between climate variables during the Pleistocene glacial cycles. We quantify the behavior of these time series using multifractal time-weighted detrended fluctuation analysis, which differentiates between near-red-noise and white-noise behavior below and above the 100 000-year glacial cycle, respectively, in all records. This study builds upon the work of Keyes et al. [Chaos 33, 093132 (2023)] by incorporating ice volume into a five-variable model that includes carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and temperature, along with intervariable coupling terms to capture potential relationships among these variables. To test our model, we compute response functions for each pair of variables and compare them with empirical data, confirming our predictions regarding intervariable stability and coupling. This study provides a comprehensive overview of glacial-interglacial dynamics and highlights the role of cryosphere-climate feedbacks in shaping Earth's climate evolution.

title: Sea ice variability and links to East Siberian permafrost carbon remobilization during the last glacial-interglacial transition
abstract: Sea ice is an important regulator of the Arctic climate systems. Records of sea ice past instrumental records are necessary to understand how sea ice is altered during past periods of abrupt climate change, and what consequences such changes have on the polar climates. Here, we reconstructed the sea ice cover of the East Siberian Arctic and found that the sea ice extent likely was linked to protecting/eroding permafrost coastlines during the last deglaciation.

title: Did temperate trees survive the Last Glacial Maximum in the North Sea Basin? A critical review of current evidence
abstract: ABSTRACT The hypothesis that temperate tree taxa survived the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM; 26.5–19 ka cal BP) in cryptic northern refugia has significant implications for European biogeography and postglacial vegetation history. Recently, sedimentary ancient DNA recovered from offshore sediment cores in the Southern River System of the North Sea Basin has been interpreted as evidence for the local persistence of temperate woodland taxa during the LGM. This review critically evaluates that hypothesis by synthesising the currently available palaeobotanical and sedimentary ancient DNA evidence from the North Sea Basin and adjacent terrestrial regions. Independent palaeoclimate reconstructions consistently indicate cold, dry conditions, continuous permafrost and temperatures well below the ecological requirements of temperate woodland trees. These reconstructions are broadly congruent with pollen, plant macrofossil, vertebrate and coleopteran records, which collectively indicate the persistence of low‐productivity arctic to subarctic steppe–tundra vegetation throughout the region during the LGM. This strong convergence among independent palaeoenvironmental datasets contrasts with limited support for the local persistence of temperate woodland communities throughout the LGM in the North Sea Basin.

title: Intra-annual grounding-line migration and retreat: insights from high-resolution satellite and in situ observations over Milne Glacier in the Canadian High Arctic
abstract: Arctic glaciers that flow into the ocean are changing rapidly due to climate warming. The grounding line, where these glaciers transition from land to ocean, is critical to their stability. We examined Milne Glacier in the Canadian High Arctic using satellite, field, and modelled data. Our study shows how changes in ice flow and ice bending near the grounding line affect satellite-based mapping of this area and documents a newly discovered grounding-line retreat associated with subglacial ridges.

title: Landscape evolution at an emerging englacial esker in Southeast Iceland over weekly-to-annual timescales
abstract: Abstract Eskers are used to characterize glacial drainage systems to inform ice-sheet modeling. However, the connection between eskers preserved in the paleoglaciologic record and the conditions required to deposit them is not well understood, particularly for englacial eskers. We use uncrewed aerial vehicle data over weekly-to-annual timescales from 2021 to 2024 at Breiðamerkurjökull in Iceland to investigate how englacial eskers evolve after emerging from the glacier. During the study period, an esker emerged from an englacial conduit, experienced significant modification and was emplaced on the outwash plain at the edge of a proglacial lake. We find that englacial eskers experience significant erosion and modification as they interact with proglacial lakes or streams and their ice cores melt, implying that englacial eskers are not generally well preserved in the paleoglaciologic record. Both esker morphology and stratigraphy evolved over the study period, indicating that when observed in preserved englacial eskers, they do not necessarily reflect conduit emplacement conditions. Englacial eskers deposited at the edge of overdeepenings may be more likely to be preserved than those deposited elsewhere. Additionally, surface ice topography evolution is assessed to identify structural hazards at an esker-forming glacier margin, which is critical as glacial-related hazards increase in a warming climate.

title: Ice‐Sheet–Ocean Interactions and the Reversibility of a Regime Shift Beneath Filchner‐Ronne Ice Shelf
abstract: Abstract Future atmospheric warming could cause an abrupt increase in ocean temperature beneath the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf, Antarctica, from −2.2°C to more than 0°C in a few decades. In simulations, such a transition leads to a twenty‐fold increase in sub‐shelf melt rates, driving a retreat of the ice sheet. Here we investigate the evolution and reversibility of the ocean and ice sheet states using coupled ice‐sheet–ocean model simulations. We show that sub‐shelf melt rates increase only half as much as in the uncoupled system, and we find that, after a period of climate cooling, the cavity is reversible from warm to cold conditions, independently of ice‐ocean interactions related to regional changes in sub‐shelf melting, cavity geometry, and ocean dynamics. In contrast to the abrupt warming transition, the recovery of a cold ocean state takes more than a century. Meanwhile the ice sheet continues to lose mass and contribute to sea level rise with a maximum rate of up to 0.9 mm/a.

title: Research progress on the geomorphic evolution of the Taihu Lake Basin since the LGM and its implications for the human living environment
abstract: The coupling between Neolithic cultural vicissitudes and paleogeomorphic evolution is a core issue in environmental archaeological research in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River. Based on a synthesis and analysis of advances in environmental archaeology over the past few decades, the study systematically reviews and evaluates key scientific issues such as sea-level changes in eastern China since the Last Glacial Maximum, the geomorphic evolution processes in the Taihu Lake Basin, and their impacts on the distribution of Neolithic sites, with a focus on discussing controversial issues such as the existence of the Holocene high sea-level stand, the genesis of the “present-day Taihu Lake”, and the causes of the collapse of the Liangzhu culture. In addition, by synthesizing the prehistoric subsistence strategies, the study offers new insights into the prospection of Neolithic sites predating 7 ka BP. The results demonstrate that the sea-level in East China commenced a period of rapid rise following the end of the LGM. The rate of rise then decreased at ∼7 ka BP, shifting to a slower rise phase with subsequent fluctuating upward trends. A mid-Holocene high sea-level stand occurred during ∼7–4 ka BP, with sea-level ∼2 m higher than present-day level. Furthermore, the geomorphic evolution of the Taihu Lake Basin stems from the long-term superimposition and coupling of multiple driving factors. It underwent successive stages of “paleosurface formation”, “hummocky terrace formation”, “chenier ridge formation”, and “dish-shaped depression formation”. During ∼7–3 ka BP, the area experienced a geomorphic reversal stage, evolving from a hummocky terrace toward a lake-plain landscape centered on dish-shaped depressions. The spatial distribution of Neolithic sites in this region closely responds to geomorphic and environmental changes, revealing a distinct human migration pattern: settlements shifted from uplands to plains and subsequently to high coastal areas. The collapse of the Liangzhu culture was primarily triggered by frequent flooding events, which were jointly induced by ENSO-enhanced precipitation variability and sea-level rise under cold and dry climatic conditions. Neolithic sites predating 7 ka BP may be preserved on elevated terraces and paleochannel terraces formed during the terminal LGM.

title: A large ice‐dammed lake in the western Danish North Sea: Deglacial evolution and ice‐margin dynamics
abstract: Abstract The Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) ice extent in the western Danish North Sea remains unchartered, which impedes our understanding of the last glacial to Holocene transition in the region. Despite increasing interest in the shallow subsurface of the North Sea, there is still a knowledge gap concerning this transition. In this study, we describe the geological evolution of the southern part of the western Danish North Sea using high‐resolution seismic data, with emphasis on the LGM and the late Quaternary development. We have identified a large glaciotectonic complex that delineates the maximum extent of the LGM ice sheet and indicates a general NNW‐SSE ice flow direction. We describe the drainage history associated with a large ice‐dammed lake, which covered most of the southern North Sea, presumably lasting for more than 2000 years from the LGM until ~19 cal kyrs BP. Based on the interpreted seismic profiles and regional depositional and deformational patterns, we provide a model for how the deglaciation unfolded in the western Danish North Sea. The deglacial sequence of events is placed into a late Quaternary context and related to the existing stratigraphic models for the area. Our study sheds new light on the distribution of potentially challenging buried landscapes for offshore construction and windfarm development.

title: The Radiative Forcing Model Intercomparison Project (RFMIP2.0) for CMIP7
abstract: Abstract. An external perturbation to the climate system from anthropogenic or natural activity first impacts the climate by inducing a perturbation to Earth’s energy budget, known as a radiative forcing. The characteristics of the radiative forcing, such as its global-mean magnitude and spatial pattern, determine the subsequent climate response. Therefore, forming accurate projections of climate change first requires diagnosing radiative forcing and evaluating its persistent uncertainty in Global Climate Models. As part of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 7 (CMIP7), the second iteration of the Radiative Forcing Model Intercomparison Project (RFMIP2.0) will enable the systematic characterization of effective radiative forcing and its components across state-of-the-art climate models, through a set of fixed-Sea Surface Temperature timeslice and transient experiments. The protocol for RFMIP2.0, introduced here, will in part serve as a continuity and an expansion of core RFMIP experiments first introduced in CMIP6, some of which have now been incorporated into the overarching CMIP7 DECK and FastTrack protocols given their broad utility. This will allow for a consistent estimate for radiative forcing across multiple model generations, which is valuable for model evaluation and future development. RFMIP2.0 also includes new experiments that will address open questions about the definition of radiative forcing, such as its sensitivity to evolving surface conditions, and will further enhance an ever-growing swath of science applications that rely on an understanding of Earth’s energy budget.

title: Extreme cold–dry events in East Asia during glacials reflect insolation thresholds
abstract: Abstract Whether extreme climate events reflect intrinsic threshold behaviour of the climate system remains uncertain, in part because most terrestrial archives integrate multiple climatic signals and lack simultaneous constraints on temperature and hydroclimate. Here we present high-resolution ( ~ 900 years) quantitative reconstructions of land temperature and monsoon precipitation from the Chinese Loess Plateau spanning the past ~250,000 years, based on molecular fossil proxies. Using branched glycerol dialkyl glycerol tetraether (brGDGT) proxies for temperature and precipitation, together with complementary GDGT-based aridity indicators, our records reveal repeated extreme cold–dry events during glacial inceptions, in addition to pronounced droughts during glacial terminations. Although previous studies have provided key insights into past monsoon variability, these cold–dry extremes are not clearly expressed in widely used terrestrial proxies such as speleothem δ¹⁸O records, indicating that key aspects of continental climate variability have remained under-recognized. Transient climate simulations reproduce the timing of the extreme cooling events, providing model-based support for threshold-like climate responses to declining boreal summer insolation. Our findings suggest that such threshold-like behaviour may represent an important mode of continental climate responses to orbital forcing, providing a long-term perspective for assessing how regional climate extremes may emerge when background conditions approach critical thresholds.

title: Improved subglacial boundary conditions near Dome C, Antarctica, through rigorous integration of multi-campaign radar data and an ensemble stochastic simulation approach
abstract: We map new details of the landscape beneath the Antarctic Ice Sheet near Dome C using radar data and simulation methods. The terrain is rougher than previously thought, and we identify where water flow is either well or poorly understood. We also show that valleys and ridges could amplify or reduce geothermal heating, impacting melting at the ice sheet base. These results improve confidence in locating sites where ancient ice may be preserved for drilling and studying past climates.

title: Summer subsurface temperature variability in the percolation zone of southwest Greenland: high resolution observations of the top meter of firn
abstract: Understanding energetic processes at the surface is important for understanding how the Greenland ice sheet melts. However, most temperature observations of firn are insufficient for studying energetic processes near the surface where melt happens. In this work we present new ground observations of high-resolution temperature profiles in the top meter of firn near the southwest coast of Greenland. Using these observations we characterize how temperature and energy vary during the melt season.

title: The implementation and effectiveness of Calving Algorithms in numerical ice models (CalvingMIP)
abstract: Ice calving is a recent inclusion in ice sheet models and there has not been a systematic test of how well it has been implemented. We show that models can accurately represent a given rate of ice calving, properties at the ice front evolve smoothly during calving, and that there are no consistent differences in ice behaviour between various approaches to representing calving in numerical ice models. This gives us confidence in their ability for use in sea level rise prediction simulations.

title: Evidence for subglacial flooding in labyrinthine channels on Devon Island, Nunavut, Canada
abstract: We describe the morphological characteristics of anastomosing (labyrinthine) bedrock channels to enhance the current understanding of subglacial meltwater dynamics of the Innuitian Ice Sheet. Our work reveals a morphological similarity between labyrinthine channels and other landscapes modified by glacial floods. We argue that the presence of anastomosis, distinct erosional surfaces, and longitudinal profile slope breaks imply formation by short-lived episodes of erosion associated with floods.

title: Early warning of critical transitions: Distinguishing tipping points from turing destabilizations
abstract: Current early warning signs for tipping points often fail to distinguish between catastrophic shifts and less dramatic state changes, such as spatial pattern formation. This paper introduces a novel method that addresses this limitation by providing more information about the type of bifurcation being approached starting from a spatially homogeneous system state. This method relies on estimates of the dispersion relation from noisy spatio-temporal data, which reveals whether the system is approaching a spatially homogeneous (tipping) or spatially heterogeneous (Turing patterning) bifurcation. Using a modified Klausmeier model, we validate this method on synthetic data, exploring its performance under varying conditions including noise properties and distance to bifurcation. We also determine the data requirements for optimal performance. Our results indicate the promise of a new spatial early warning system built on this method to improve predictions of future transitions in many climate subsystems and ecosystems, which is critical for effective conservation and management in a rapidly changing world.

title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
abstract: The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

title: Surface melt variability over the Shackleton Ice Shelf from high-resolution sentinel-1 sar observations during 2015–2023
A 1 km gridded dataset of Northern Hemisphere permafrost active layer thickness (2000–2024)
abstract: Thawing permafrost accelerates global warming and threatens infrastructure, yet tracking changes over vast areas remains difficult. We combined over two decades of ground observations with artificial intelligence to create a continuous, highly detailed yearly map of permafrost thaw depth across the Northern Hemisphere from 2000 to 2024. Overcoming previous mapping limitations, this reliable dataset provides a vital tool to evaluate environmental hazards and protect vulnerable regions.

title: Oxygen isotopes reveal a significant Middle Pleistocene transition from temperate rainforest to arid desert-like conditions in eastern Australia
abstract: Reconstructing terrestrial palaeoenvironmental change during the Middle Pleistocene is essential for understanding ecosystem stability and resilience under long-term climatic forcing. However, well-dated, quantitative records from Australia remain limited. Fossil deposits at Mount Etna Caves, central eastern Queensland, preserve two taxonomically distinct faunal assemblages that have been interpreted as a substantial ecological transition from a diverse rainforest system to an arid-adapted faunal community. Previous interpretations of this transition have relied primarily on faunal evidence, with limited site-specific geochemical validation. Here, we integrate oxygen isotope (δ 18 O) analyses of fossil macropodid enamel with refined in-situ U-Th geochronology to reconstruct changes in hydroclimatic conditions across this transition. New U-Th ages better constrain deposition of the arid-adapted assemblage to a narrow interval between 199 ± 5 and 205 ± 4 ka. Fossils from older deposits (pre-280 ka) exhibit consistently low δ 18 O values (−2.59 ± 0.54 ‰), suggesting relatively humid conditions, whereas the younger deposit is markedly enriched (4.59 ± 1.92 ‰). Random Forest classification models trained on modern macropodine δ 18 O data suggest that pre-280 ka assemblages show strongest similarity with humid temperate forest environments analogous to modern temperate oceanic (Cfb-like) systems of southeastern Australia and highland New Guinea. In contrast, the post-205 ka assemblages show the strongest affinity with arid, hot desert (BWh-like) conditions characteristic of central Australia. This transition coincides with broader Middle Pleistocene climatic reorganisation centred on ∼270 ka, which may have contributed to sustained regional drying. These findings suggest that long-term climatic forcing may push ecosystems beyond hydroclimatic thresholds, resulting in major ecological reorganisation, altered species distributions, and reduced biogeographic connectivity. By providing a directly dated, multi-proxy terrestrial record, this study highlights how substantial environmental change during the Quaternary offers an important analogue for understanding ecosystem vulnerability under ongoing and future climate change.

title: Development of a semi-persistent floating terminus at San Quintín Glacier (Northern Patagonia Icefield), the last piedmont glacier in the Andes
abstract: Abstract The piedmont lobe of San Quintín Glacier, the largest outlet of the Northern Patagonia Icefield, has recently entered a phase of rapid frontal retreat. We present results from a helicopter-borne ground-penetrating radar (GPR) survey conducted in May 2019 in the terminal zone of the glacier, combined with satellite-derived ice velocity, frontal position and surface elevation change data. GPR measurements along the flowline indicate ice thicknesses of 215–240 m in the lowermost 1400 m of the glacier. The inferred grounding line is located approximately 1500 m upstream from the 2019 calving front. Analysis of surface elevation change in 2017–19 shows mean thinning rates of -5.43 plus or minus $\pm$ ± 1.58 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 upstream and -1.08 plus or minus $\pm$ ± 1.39 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 near the terminus. Satellite-derived velocities reach up to 1050 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 in the lower glacier, with higher values observed in the later part of the observation period. Residual bed reflection power derived from the GPR profiles indicates the presence of water at the glacier bed in the terminal zone. Taken together, these observations are consistent with the development of a semi-persistent floating terminus, where basal water and buoyancy modulate surface elevation change and control frontal stability and calving style. The results provide new observational constraints on the transient behaviour of floating termini at fast-flowing outlet glaciers in lacustrine settings.

title: Early pliocene warming and ocean circulation: Non-linear responses to CO2 and Central American Seaway changes in HadCM3
High-Resolution Cyclostratigraphy Uncovers Variable Orbital Forcing in the Oligocene South China Sea
abstract: The Oligocene provides an important interval for examining climatic and sedimentary variability following the Eocene–Oligocene transition, but the expression of orbital forcing in low-latitude marginal seas remains incompletely understood. We integrate natural gamma-ray (GR) logging and microfossil records from Well L9 in the Pearl River Mouth Basin, northern South China Sea, to establish a cyclostratigraphic framework spanning approximately 34.6–21.7 Ma. A floating chronology based on 405 kyr cycle counting was anchored using an independently constrained Oligocene–Miocene boundary horizon. Spectral analyses identify approximately 405 kyr, 100 kyr, and 40 kyr components, together with longer-period variability near 2.4 Myr and 1.2 Myr. Amplitude-modulation analysis reveals an approximately 1.2 Myr component in the 40 kyr envelope, supporting an obliquity-related interpretation. In contrast, the 100 kyr envelope contains approximately 1.6 Myr variability rather than a clear 2.4 Myr component, leaving the eccentricity-modulation origin of the latter unresolved. Palynological evidence indicates generally cool and humid conditions during the early–middle Oligocene, followed by late Oligocene warming. Comparison with published climate records suggests correspondence with six recognized cooling episodes, although chronological uncertainty limits precise event alignment. These results provide a regional chronological and paleoenvironmental framework and highlight the need to distinguish observed long-period sedimentary variability from its proposed orbital origin.

title: Extreme glacier melt on the Central Tibetan Plateau during the summer of 2022: detection and mechanisms
abstract: Extreme glacier melt events accelerate mass loss, increase glacier instability, and temporarily increase downstream runoff, potentially alleviating drought conditions. Yet the glacier energy–mass balance in the Geladandong region – a headwater region of the Yangtze River (China's longest river) and one of the source regions feeding Siling Co (Tibet's largest lake) – and its connection to the unprecedented 2022 summer melt remain insufficiently quantified. To address this gap, we integrated in-situ mass balance observations and glacio-meteorological data from a 5700 m monitoring site with an energy-mass balance model and applied a novel dual-threshold framework (based on mean and standard deviation) to identify extreme mass loss/melt events in short-term glacier mass balance records. Our novel methodology identified 2021/22 as a period of extreme mass loss and melt intensity, with melt during the 2022 summer heatwave reaching unprecedented extremes. These heatwaves caused an increase in melt amount of 317.8 mm w.e., amounting to 1.66 and 1.69 times the values recorded for the same period in 2019/20 and 2020/21, respectively. This extreme melt was driven by energy balance anomalies over the glacier surface. In terms of net contributions to the +28.2 W m −2 melt energy anomaly during the three identified heatwave windows, enhanced sensible heat flux was the largest term (+17.0 W m −2 ; 60.3 %), followed by increased net longwave radiation (+14.0 W m −2 ; 49.7 %) and increased net shortwave radiation (+5.1 W m −2 ; 18.1 %) associated with reduced albedo, with negative contributions from latent heat flux and subsurface heat flux. Such anomalies were driven by large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns, specifically the eastward extension and northward displacement of the South Asian High (SAH), together with near-neutral mid-latitude westerlies. This study advances the understanding of glacier mass balance responses to extreme weather and climate events on the central Tibetan Plateau.

title: Tree-ring cellulose oxygen isotope reveals summer hydroclimate variability across the East European Plain
abstract: Along the East European Plain latitudinal transect, Scots pine tree-ring cellulose oxygen isotopes (δ18OTRC) increases from north to south and consistently records significant summer hydroclimate signals. Although the dominant controls differ among regions, the northern chronology shows the strongest and most stable vapor pressure deficit signal. Compared with tree-ring width (TRW), δ18OTRC better reflects regional climate information linked to atmospheric humidity and evaporative demand.

title: DDA-BNN v1.0: a morphology-aware surrogate model for  the optical properties of black carbon-containing particles
abstract: We developed a surrogate model to predict how black carbon particles absorb and scatter light based on their size, shape, and mixing with other aerosol species. The model was trained on detailed physics simulations and also estimates uncertainty caused by limited training data and unresolved internal structures. It outperformed common simplified particle assumptions, especially for scattering, and can help target new simulations to improve predictions of black carbon's radiative effects.

title: Divergent Evolution Patterns of Glacier Meltwater and Implications for Downstream Water Utilization in Inland River Basins of the Northern Tibetan Plateau During 1976–2024
abstract: The controls on glacier meltwater change and their implications for water supply risks remain unclear in glacier-fed inland river basins. We reconstructed glacier meltwater changes during 1976–2024 in eight representative basins of the northern Tibetan Plateau using a degree-day factor model and assessed its contribution to mountain-outlet runoff and downstream water use. Independent evaluation using the 2018 glacier inventory showed relative errors of 0.34–9.85% across the eight basins. Glacier storage decreased in all basins after the basin-specific segmentation years, while meltwater increased in most basins but declined in the Yarkand River Basin. These contrasting responses highlight substantial spatial differences in glacier meltwater evolution despite widespread glacier storage loss and increasing summer temperatures. The multi-year mean contribution of glacier meltwater to mountain-outlet runoff ranged from 1.2% to 54.3% across the eight basins, with declining contributions after the segmentation years in several highly glacierized basins. In the Hexi Corridor, annual glacier meltwater in the Shule River Basin was equivalent to about 20–40% of downstream water use. Glacier meltwater contributions to low-flow runoff increased in the three Hexi Corridor basins and in the Golmud and Buha River basins, but decreased in the Yarkand and Hotan River basins. These findings suggest potential implications of glacier storage loss for low-flow support and seasonal water supply risks, particularly in basins with substantial downstream irrigation and ecological water demands.

title: Sequential high-density radiocarbon dating to detect invisible event layers in marine sediments
abstract: Abstract We present a unique application of radiocarbon measurements on hemipelagic sediments that uses continuous radiocarbon dating of total organic carbon ( 14 C TOC age) to recognize event deposits. The 14 C TOC age of sediments is not commonly used for age determination because total organic carbon includes various origins, such as marine, terrestrial, and reworked old fragments. In this study, the 14 C TOC ages of some horizons were found to be older than those of the deeper ones through continuous 14 C TOC measurements at 0.5- to 1.0-cm intervals. The reversal 14 C TOC ages resulted not from the settlement of organic particles from the terrestrial environments, such as floodings, but from the submarine slope failures. Therefore, we can regard the reversal 14 C TOC layers as event layers due to geohazards. After reconstruction of the age model using foraminiferal tests obtained from the sediment core used in this study, depositional ages of event layers were identified. Well correlation with historical natural disasters after the 15 th century suggest validity of the method proposed by the current study.

title: Observed warming and moistening trend over South Asia in recent decades consistent with CMIP6 multi-model simulations
abstract: Abstract Under global warming, land surfaces have warmed substantially faster than the oceans, leading to widespread drying across most continental regions. However, across South Asia, an anomalous trend of moistening, indicated by an increase in surface relative humidity (RH), has been observed in recent decades despite continued land-surface warming. We find that this moistening pattern is consistently evident in multiple observational, reanalysis, and station-based datasets and is also present in the CMIP6 multi-model mean, indicating that the observed moistening trend is broadly consistent with the externally forced response simulated by CMIP6. These concurrent warming and moistening trends have important implications for humid-heat conditions relevant to human health, as higher RH under a warming climate can significantly reduce heat dissipation and exacerbate heat stress. We further evaluate these humid-heat implications using wet-bulb temperature and heat index. This study further discusses the possible mechanisms behind the anomalous moistening trend, focusing on the monsoon season, and highlights enhanced moisture convergence as a dynamically consistent and physically plausible contributor to the increase in surface RH under warming. The broad consistency between the observed trends and the CMIP6 multi-model mean suggests an important role for the externally forced climate response and provides a basis for future assessments of whether the South Asian moistening trend may persist or intensify under continued anthropogenic forcing. Such assessments should nevertheless account for the influences of internal variability, regional processes, and remaining model biases.

title: Quaternary Palm Fossils from Coastal Florida, USA: A 2016 Hurricane as a Tool for Paleontology Research
abstract: In October 2016, Hurricane Matthew passed along the east coast of Florida, USA. Intense coastal erosion by storm waves made sandy beaches to reveal a multitude of trunk molds of ancient palm trees that once flourished along what is now the intertidal zone. A combination of coastal engineering efforts and natural processes caused the ancient palms to be reburied by beach sand. Fortunately, two retired geologists quickly responded after the hurricane ended, conducting a detailed investigation of the fossil palms. The trunk molds occur in two adjacent parallel zones that have an overall length of 1.4 km. The seaward-facing zone contains trunk molds where wood has been mineralized by calcite, enclosed within a coquinoid outer zone. The molds are associated with areas of gray coquina. In contrast, the landward-facing zone is characterized by trunk molds that contain mummified wood tissues within a weakly cemented sand matrix. These molds have thin coquina outer boundaries, but they occur within loose beach sand. Geological and botanical characteristics suggest a Holocene age for the ancient palm groves; their occurrence and demise are associated with small-scale regression/transgression cycles. A 14C radiocarbon age of 160 yrs BP for one of the younger cycles suggests the possibility that the landward- facing coastal palm growth was related to tidal changes that were related to the temperature fluctuations of the Little Ice Age (1300–1850).

title: Short-Campaign GNSS Observations of Horizontal Velocity and Vertical Tidal Response Across the Drygalski Ice Tongue, East Antarctica
abstract: The Drygalski Ice Tongue is a tide-influenced floating extension of the David Glacier in East Antarctica, where field observations are constrained by polar logistics. We investigated how horizontal ice motion and vertical tidal response vary along and across the tongue. To extend earlier observations, we analysed a 2025–2026 Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) campaign comprising 12 stations and 248 station-days. Kinematic GNSS coordinate series were produced with Bernese 5.4 and subsequently analysed under four stochastic covariance descriptions for horizontal and apparent vertical-rate estimation. Comparisons with a regional Mario Zucchelli Station (MZS)/Terra Nova Bay tide reference characterized station-level up-component response to tidal forcing, and two tide-removal paths were evaluated for apparent vertical-rate analysis. Floating-tongue speeds increased downstream, spanning 663.9–749.4 m/yr, with a clockwise turn toward the southeast and north-to-south differences in fitted campaign rates. The main horizontal patterns persisted across all four tested covariance descriptions. Vertical tidal response was weak in the near-grounding group, spatially heterogeneous in the transition sector, and near-unity downstream. Across the four covariance descriptions, neither tide-removal approach yielded a model-robust apparent vertical-rate field. The campaign resolved spatial patterns of horizontal motion and vertical tidal response, while covariance testing identified the limits of apparent vertical-rate inference from short GNSS records.

title: Tracking danger on the peaks
abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

title: Ground-Penetrating Radar Ice-Thickness Survey and 3D Bed-Topography Modelling of the Weigele Glacier Constrained by Borehole-Calibrated Radar Velocity
abstract: Glacier thickness and subglacial bed topography are fundamental parameters for ice-volume estimation of mountain glaciers; in regions where direct field observations are sparse, these parameters remain weakly constrained in space. This study deployed a closed-loop ground-penetrating radar (GPR) survey network on Weigele Glacier in the Animaqing Mountains and calibrated the radar wave velocity using a GPR profile that crossed an in situ borehole. The borehole-calibrated effective radar wave velocity is 0.17018 m·ns−1, which is 1.30% higher than the commonly used default value of 0.168 m·ns−1. Based on 1477 GPR ice-thickness measurements and zero-thickness boundary points at the upper glacier margin, Gaussian process regression was used to interpolate ice thickness on a 5 m horizontal grid. Leave-one-profile-out cross-validation showed that adding the ice-surface slope covariate changed the model error only slightly (RMSE of 85.48 m) relative to the coordinate-only baseline model (RMSE of 85.44 m); the final reconstruction therefore adopted horizontal coordinates as predictors. Within the 0.481 km2 GPR modelling domain, the maximum measured ice thickness is 258.328 m, the mean interpolated ice thickness is 130.10 m, and the ice volume is 0.06260 km3. The reconstructed bed exhibits a pronounced longitudinal trough, and the low-lying bed corresponds spatially to the main thick-ice zone. Boundary-condition sensitivity tests yield an ice-volume range of 0.04767–0.07531 km3. These volume estimates correspond to the modelling domain covered by the GPR network.

title: Historical Multidecadal Variability of Intraseasonal Features of Sahel Rainfall in CMIP6 Models and Observations
abstract: Abstract We compare observations with seven large ensembles of CMIP6 historical simulations to understand the role that external forcings and internal variability may have played in modulating the frequency and intensity of daily rainfall, and the duration of the rainy season in the Sahel. We compare three periods: [1950–1970], [1970–1990] and [1994–2014]. The results show that the anomalously wet [1950–1970] and [1994–2014] periods are characterized by more extreme rainfall days and longer monsoon seasons than the drier [1970–1990] period. In exploring the contributions of anthropogenic aerosols (AAs) and greenhouse gases (GHGs) in both transitions, we find results to be consistent with partial cancellation of the effects of AA and GHG in the [1950–1970] to [1970–1990] transition to drought, which allows internal variability to contribute significantly, and with the emergence of the external forcing effect in the [1970–1990] to [1994–2014] recovery. In particular, the shift of AA emissions from North America and Europe to Asia between [1970–1990] and [1994–2014] increases the number of extreme rainy days and lengthens the wet season. The increase in GHG concentrations between these two periods also acts to increase the number of extreme rainy days. However, this effect is not statistically significant in all models. Finally, in all the models analyzed, we cannot discard the fact that the individual effects of AAs and GHGs add up linearly in setting the total precipitation change.

title: Observational data and neural network-accelerated modelling provide valuable insights for glacier thickness reconstruction in High Mountain Asia
abstract: We estimate the thickness of a glacier in the Himalaya, using recently available thickness measurements and a computational model which uses higher-order physics to match thickness with satellite-observed velocity. Our velocity-constrained estimate achieves similar accuracy to leading estimates, while estimates additionally constrained by thickness show increased accuracy, but limited interpolative power. We make recommendations for future measurement locations and for choosing model parameters.

title: Topographic controls on glacier Equilibrium Line Altitudes
abstract: Glacier Equilibrium Line Altitudes (ELAs) are substantially influenced by topography through processes such as preferential shading, avalanching, or snow redistribution by wind. Here, we present a novel framework with which these topographic controls can be better assessed. The approach involves (1) estimating the ELA from glacier outlines and surface geometries, (2) separating the ELA into a regional climatic average (regELA) and a local topographic residual (ΔELA) via spatial autocorrelation, and (3) correlating ΔELA to terrain parameters characterizing the shape and orientation of glaciers and their catchments. The framework is developed and calibrated using the Swiss Glacier Inventory (SGI) 2016. In the SGI2016, the average absolute ΔELA is around 200 m, and shows significant correlations with potential solar radiation, topographic openness, ice surface curvature, and the relative size of a glacier’s catchment. These terrain parameters are then used to train a random forest-based regression model, which accurately predicts ΔELA for each Swiss glacier (R2 = 0.95) but can also be successfully transferred to earlier inventories within the Swiss Alps (R2 = 0.59 to 0.73). A spatial transfer, on the other hand, works only for regions with similar topographic and glaciological characteristics like New Zealand (R2 = 0.59), while a transfer from Switzerland to Icelandic glaciers proved unsuccessful (R2 = 0.11) and requires local recalibration. The framework developed in this study allows for a better quantification of topographic controls on present-day glaciers but can eventually also be transferred to a palaeoclimatic context, leading to improved temperature and precipitation reconstructions for past glaciations.

title: We Are in the Anthropocene—Now What?
abstract: Abstract While the term “Anthropocene” is well established across scientific disciplines and social spheres, interpretations are diverse. Taking account of the 2024 rejection by a geological commission to accept the Anthropocene as a geological epoch and the related scientific debate, here we offer a future‐oriented perspective from the viewpoint of Earth system science. We describe different pathways in the Anthropocene up to the year 3,000, systematically characterizing them according to impacts and causes. We discuss the enormous global consequences of anthropogenic pressures on the Earth system and quantify the corresponding long‐term commitment to change. Regarding the causes, we conservatively explore best‐case and middle‐of‐the road emission scenarios, in combination with climate sensitivities drawn from within the IPCC likely range. We also discuss implications for Earth system resilience that could result in what we call worst case scenarios for Anthropocene outcomes. We conclude that, beyond the slow pace of natural climate recovery spanning many millennia, even minimal, unavoidable residual emissions like from the food sector risk perpetuating global warming in the absence of other human forcing. One implication is that if climate or carbon cycle feedbacks shift toward reinforcing warming, they risk not only exacerbating climate impacts but to also surpassing human forcing in relevance. At that point, human influence on the Anthropocene would no longer play the dominant role.

title: Importance of glacier shrinkage for sustaining runoff in Panj River of Pamir, Central Asia
abstract: Study region The study area is the Panj River basin, situated in the upper reaches of the Amu Darya basin. Study focus Glacier and snowmelt runoff are vital for sustaining streamflow in the Panj River Basin, a key cryospheric water source region in Central Asia. However, the impacts of glacier retreat, snow changes, and precipitation variability on long-term runoff remain unclear under global warming. This study applied the Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV) model to quantify runoff components, including rainfall, snowmelt, and glacier runoff, and integrated the Budyko framework, scenario simulations, and glacier retreat experiments to assess runoff drivers and the hydrological response to glacier loss. New hydrological insights The results showed that total runoff, rainfall runoff, and snowmelt runoff exhibited significant decreasing trends during 1982–2020, whereas glacier runoff increased, reflecting a temporary compensation effect from enhanced glacier melt under climate warming. Meltwater runoff accounted for 67.9% of total runoff and played an important role in regulating streamflow, particularly during dry years. Attribution analysis revealed that runoff changes were mainly controlled by climatic factors (122.5%), with precipitation being the dominant driver, while human activities (−22.5%) partially offset the decline in runoff. Glacier retreat scenarios indicated that continued glacier loss would reduce summer meltwater supply and may alter the seasonal distribution of runoff, with potential implications for the stability of downstream water supply. The impacts of glacier change on mountain runoff processes and regional water resources provide a basis for understanding potential changes in downstream water availability in Central Asia.

title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
abstract: arXiv:2611.18393v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

abstract: This review article explains how scientists monitor Arctic melt ponds, which are pools of water that form on sea ice in late spring and early summer. The study highlights current knowledge gaps and identifies priorities to improve future observations and climate predictions.

abstract: Hudson Bay’s seasonal sea ice limits maritime access to the Port of Churchill, and although we know future warming will lengthen the navigable period, how quickly it will lengthen is unclear. Based on several methods for making future projections, the navigable period for the route from Churchill to the Labrador Sea has lengthened by about 4 weeks since the 1980s. title: Reach-scale LCOE of run-of-river hydropower under glacier retreat and winter ice in the Tien Shan
abstract: Run-of-river small hydropower (SHP) can electrify off-grid mountain communities in Central Asia, but national assessments rely on coarse runoff grids and fixed capacity factors. We assess 949 reaches of the glacierised Sary-Jaz basin (Tien Shan, Kyrgyzstan) by combining twelve winters of Sentinel-1 backscatter to detect river ice, a degree-day discharge model forced by ERA5-Land and CHIRPS, and a levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) framework. Energy is computed from a screening capacity factor or simulated daily flow, and uncertainty is examined with Monte Carlo, multi-SSP and lifetime analyses. Screening LCOE without ice is 72–544 USD/MWh (median 147). Without ice, the 20–50% glacier-fraction class is cheapest (139.5 USD/MWh), but SAR-derived ice derating shifts this to the 5–20% class (146.7 versus 152.3 USD/MWh). The shift persists with flow-based energy (156.8 versus 162.7 USD/MWh) and needs a shutdown fraction of only 0.00–0.14. Because simulated winter flow mostly falls below the minimum turbine flow, this derating is an upper bound; with generation-weighted derating the classes are tied at present, but the 5–20% class remains cheaper in all eight SSP snapshots. With reach-level cost uncertainty, it is cheaper in 63% of 2000 Monte Carlo realisations, a probable tendency rather than a certainty. Under SSP2-4.5, the 50–100% class loses 24% of its design discharge by 2080; its lifetime LCOE rises from 173 to 180 USD/MWh between commissioning years 2030 and 2050, whereas the 5–20% class stays near 152 USD/MWh. No reach approaches the ≈46–52 USD/MWh feed-in tariff; tariff reform or concessional finance is required.

title: The variability fingerprint of a warming world informing climate risk and solutions
abstract: Global warming has become an increasingly urgent issue that must be addressed within a limited timeframe, as the debate over the overshoot pathway intensifies. Existing climate and socio-economic models inform our understanding but are too complex for timely action and non-expert use. To address these challenges, our stochastic framework leverages a one-box Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model with colored-noise forcing to characterize variance scaling in detrended temperatures and links this behavior to an empirical Hurst coefficient. The observed weakening of anti-persistence, as summarized by this coefficient, is then used to quantify changes in temperature variance relative to the pre-industrial era. Our empirical Hurst maps reveal patterns consistent with findings from global climate models, highlighting greater changes in temperature variance in equatorial regions, such as southeastern Amazonia and western Indonesia, than in high-latitude regions. Furthermore, seasonal analyses of African temperature records reveal pronounced heterogeneity in variance changes, identifying vulnerable regions that are masked when variability is assessed at annual timescales. By linking our results to climate solutions that consider fairness in burden-sharing and unequal risk-bearing capacity, we anticipate that the empirical Hurst coefficient will support more equitable and effective climate action.

title: Discrepancies and Consistencies in Multi-Source Estimates of Eurasian Spring Snowmelt During 1982–2014
abstract: Snow alters land–atmosphere energy and moisture exchanges via albedo and hydrological effects, markedly impacting subseasonal-to-seasonal climate variability. While Earth observations and model-based products form the foundation for investigating snow–climate interactions, comprehensive assessments of snowmelt, which directly reflects snow-induced hydrological and thermal anomalies, remain scarce compared to those of conventional snow mass variables. Benchmarked against the satellite–in situ blended GlobSnow data, this study comprehensively evaluates the discrepancies and consistencies of Eurasian spring snowmelt (spring snow water equivalent difference, SSD) across six multi-source datasets (SnowCCI, JRA-3Q, ERA5-Land, MERRA-2, GLDAS-NOAH, and FLDAS) during 1982–2014. The results reveal that satellite-based SnowCCI and JRA-3Q exhibit the highest consistency with GlobSnow in reproducing the spatial distribution, temporal variability, and dominant east–west dipole mode of Eurasian SSD. Specifically, they accurately capture its clear latitudinal zonation and a distinct dipole-like trend, characterized by decreasing SSD over western Eurasia and increasing SSD over eastern Eurasia. Conversely, ERA5-Land and MERRA-2 reasonably capture the temporal evolution of SSD but tend to overestimate variability amplitudes. GLDAS-NOAH exhibits relatively weak regional heterogeneity and underestimates SSD variability, whereas FLDAS tends to overestimate variability amplitudes and shows pronounced regional dependence. Further analysis suggests that uncertainties in snowfall simulations may be a major source of discrepancies in SSD estimation, although their relative contribution remains uncertain. These findings provide crucial insights for selecting appropriate datasets in snow–climate research and underscore the importance of dataset uncertainty quantification in subseasonal-to-seasonal climate prediction.

title: A global 0.05° dataset of daily latent heat flux and resistances (2001–2020) derived via the Energy-Resistance-Coupling framework
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) We developed a daily global dataset describing latent heat flux and the resistances that regulate land–atmosphere water and energy exchange from 2001 to 2020 at 0.05° resolution. The product was evaluated against 244 flux-tower sites and performs robustly across climates and ecosystems. It provides new information for studying drought, ecosystem water stress, land–atmosphere coupling, and Earth system models.

title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Ni\~{n}o Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
abstract: arXiv:2611.17854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The predictability of the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Ni\~{n}o, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Ni\~{n}o development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
abstract: arXiv:2611.13359v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.

title: Anomalous terrigenous input to the continental margin of tropical western South Atlantic at the Pleistocene-Holocene transition
A Konso Silver Tuff correlative found offshore the East African Rift
abstract: Offshore the Horn of Africa, volcanic ash layers preserved in deep-sea sediments have played a crucial role in establishing and refining chronologies for paleontological sites in the East African Rift System (EARS). However, no such layers younger than 750 ka have been identified, despite evidence for major eruptions during this interval. Here, we investigate the 166-150 ka interval in marine sediment core MD96-2073, retrieved near Socotra Island. We constructed an age-depth model based on δ 18 O tie-points and 14 C dates, using Bayesian statistics (BACON software). This core spans at least 250 kyr, with a mean chronological uncertainty of ± 3.5 ka (95% confidence interval). Although no visible tephra layers were identified, glass-shard counting revealed a distinct cryptotephra horizon dated to 154.6 ka (13 ka as whole 95% confidence interval). Major and trace element analyses of glass shards allow correlation of this cryptotephra with the Konso Silver Tuff, which is considered to derive from the Shala volcano, making it the youngest EARS-derived tephra currently correlated with marine deposits. This cryptotephra represents a widespread tephrostratigraphic marker and provides a new chronological anchor for sediments of comparable age, including lacustrine, paleontological, and archaeological records.

title: To tip or not to tip
abstract: Tipping points have become a popular concept in earth sciences and for communicating climate risk. However, we identify three issues with existing tipping definitions that cause confusion about what "tipping" means. We propose to define a tipping event as a persistent nonlinear transition, shifting focus from abruptness and irreversibility to nonlinear response and self-amplifying feedback. We illustrate how our definition can be applied in practice to determine whether tipping occurs or not.
